Adoption of GenAI in education
While non‑generative educational AI tools have remained largely invisible to the general public (and not widely utilised 
in education), especially before the COVID pandemic, the emergence of GenAI has made AI and its possibilities visible 
to all and challenged teachers and the education sector. Contrary to most educational AI, general‑purpose GenAI tools 
are available for free outside of school and students and teachers can (and do) use them whether they are provided by 
their universities or schools or not. Contrary to most other non‑generative educational AI tools, most GenAI tools are 
not designed to support students’ learning, but to perform tasks, including learning tasks that students typically receive 
from teachers as educational assignments. As a result, the first response to the emergence of LLMs was an outcry 
about students’ academic integrity and cheating. While a small market for the outsourcing of educational assignments 
to humans existed before GenAI, this possibility suddenly became freely accessible to most. This first reaction mainly 
spoke to the “credentialing” and “sorting” function of education systems, that have to guarantee the reliability, fairness 
and comparability of grades, degrees and competence.

Insights on the effective use of generative AI in education
Chapter 14
248
OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026          © OECD 2026
As long as they have an adequate device and connectivity, students and teachers can use powerful general‑purpose 
GenAI tools. Domestic and international surveys show that students already very widely do so outside of the classroom, 
and more so as they get older. They may access GenAI in very different ways in different contexts though, and even run 
GenAI tools that work with no connectivity. A sizeable share of their parents also uses GenAI, for work and personal 
reasons. And teachers use GenAI tools to generate lesson plans, quizzes, assignments, and even sometimes to grade 
and provide feedback to their students. In some cases, they may use specialised educational GenAI tools. Academic 
staff and other scientists also increasingly use GenAI for research, often just to improve the fluidity of their English as a 
foreign language, but sometimes also to solve problems that would be impossible to solve quickly (or solve at all) without 
GenAI tools. Specialised GenAI tools have been developed for most stages of the research process, especially for natural 
sciences. GenAI has now become part of the social and educational reality and is therefore difficult to ignore. Given the 
pervasiveness of GenAI in the labour market, many call for education to foster GenAI literacy as a way to upskill and 
reskill students and professionals to effectively participate in the workforce.
Strengths and weaknesses of GenAI systems
The scientific achievement of a specialised scientific generative AI system, AlphaFold, gives a good example of the 
possibilities of GenAI tools: within a year, the model generated the 3D shape of 200 million proteins based on their 
molecular composition, virtually all that were known so far. Its inventors were awarded the Nobel Prize in chemistry in 
2024. Before then, it took (usually a PhD student) three years to generate the shape of a single protein. This scientific 
breakthrough has opened new possibilities in medicine to develop drugs and refocused human research on more 
complex scientific problems in structural chemistry. GenAI tools go beyond helping us to retrieve knowledge, they also 
contribute to knowledge production and productivity.
What is so special about general-purpose GenAI tools, which are typically experienced through chatbots? They often 
provide pertinent and contextualised answers to questions, with the ability to clarify and ask follow‑up questions, in 
ways that were not possible before with (non‑generative AI) natural language processing. LLMs are trained on and 
access data that exceeds what humans could retrieve. Moreover, they are flexible and can be applied to many different 
subjects, even though emerging research shows that narrow or specialised AI tools usually outperform general‑purpose 
AI on the narrow tasks for which they were designed. In the case of education, this is for example the case for scoring 
assessment tasks. Finally, general‑purpose GenAI tools can be turned into educational tools or combined with previous 
educational AI to enhance them with generative functionalities. 
A series of well‑known shortcomings are also specific to current GenAI, and are inherent to its technology, thus applying 
to some extent to all its derivatives. Because they are based on probabilistic models, they can “hallucinate”, that is, 
provide a wrong but plausible answer or invent some elements of the answer. They do not produce consistent results 
over time: asked to perform the same task several times, they will come up with different answers or productions, 
which is sometimes welcome, sometimes not. This may be because of regular system updates by providers, but mainly 
because of their probabilistic nature. And because they are trained on available datasets, their answers and other 
productions tend to reproduce the views and perspectives represented in those datasets, which are overwhelmingly 
based on English‑speaking (and Western) cultures. For example, they may lack “representative accuracy” and fail to 
reflect the specific cultural and linguistic heritage of the local community in which they are used. As a result, their outputs 
require human supervision and scrutiny, and often more so than specialised, non‑generative AI systems. 
GenAI comes with a series of societal challenges that can also be highlighted. Large data centres on which AI depends, 
require large amounts of energy and water. One longer term impact of GenAI also lies in the inclusion and dissemination 
of AI‑generated information and data in AI training datasets, which might either decrease the quality of future generated 
content or amplify some current limitations of our knowledge. This will make critical thinking and the development 
of metacognitive and higher‑order thinking skills even more important than before. And as is the case for education, 
understanding is still emerging of how GenAI might transform societies and economies – as well as human cognition.
Opportunities and challenges for education
Like non‑generative AI tools, the availability of GenAI tools creates both challenges and opportunities for education.
The ease with which students can use GenAI to perform assigned tasks is a challenge to education processes and 
systems, at least when students’ motivation to learn is faltering. The assumption that students’ work was evidence 
of learning and mastery does not necessarily hold when GenAI tools might have done it for them. For example, as 
automatic foreign language translators became remarkably more accurate in the past decades students were able 
to quickly perform traditional tasks of foreign language education such as translating to and from a foreign language 

Chapter 14
Insights on the effective use of generative AI in education
249
© OECD 2026          OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026 
with no or little associated learning. Similarly, the emergence of general‑purpose GenAI tools could lead to a possible 
confusion between the successful performance of an educational task (an essay, for example) and the acquisition of 
the underlying content and procedural knowledge to accomplish this task. According to research on learning, learning 
happens when students actively (and often socially) work hard in a zone of proximal development, at the edge of what 
they already know and can do. Some uses of GenAI keep them out of that zone, rather than optimising how much 
time they spend in it. It will be important to minimise the risk of the use of GenAI tools undermining the acquisition 
of important knowledge, as well as complex and personal thinking abilities such as writing, analysing, interpreting, or 
appreciating the world. This also applies to teachers, education staff or policy makers when using GenAI tools to perform 
tasks whose value lies in the process as much as in the output of the task (e.g. an institution’s “strategic plan”). 
GenAI tools also bring opportunities to the education sector, for improvement of teaching and learning as well as 
for the efficient and equitable administration of institutions and systems. One of the main benefits of AI in education 
lies in the personalisation of education, mainly for students, but also for teachers and administrators. In this context, 
personalisation means adapting learning tasks to individual needs, which can be fully balanced with collective education 
and the socialisation goal of education. In some cases, students can even perform adapted tasks while learning 
collectively. GenAI tools contribute to this agenda and can, for example, help students engage in a conversational way 
with intelligent tutoring systems that personalise educational tasks and feedback based on their current knowledge, 
level of engagement and other characteristics. Teachers can also benefit from GenAI tools to contextualise and adapt 
their lessons to their students’ interests or to receive feedback on their own teaching practices. GenAI could enable 
stakeholders to retrieve learning‑analytics data by them asking questions in natural language, to explore the data 
further through follow‑up questions that matter to them rather than the designers, and to obtain guidance on how 
such insights might inform action.
GenAI tools can also enhance education beyond personalisation. They allow for easier access to knowledge than search 
engines, by providing ready‑made summaries, and even some level of analysis of the retrieved Internet information 
(which can include incorrect information). Educational GenAI offers the possibility to learn conversationally at any time of 
the day. In many cases, these tools are becoming a new layer added to non‑generative educational AI tools, allowing for 
a more fluid natural language interface. GenAI also allows students to have educational experiences they could not have 
before, such as conversing with “digital personas” that roleplay different views and experiences or getting immediate 
feedback on their argumentation or on their writing style. Students learning in a second language or rural students can 
use GenAI tools for explanation or clarification when human support is not available.
In this context, education policy makers, institution leaders and other education stakeholders have to balance these 
opportunities and challenges. They may be tempted to prevent or delay as much as possible the use of GenAI tools so 
as to avoid the possible risks of GenAI on a precautionary basis. The unsupervised use of GenAI tools outside of school 
might still be difficult to prevent and does affect teaching, learning, assessment, and the comparability and fairness of 
education. Mastering the use of GenAI is also becoming a workforce development imperative. At some point in their 
educational journey, education systems will have to prepare students to use GenAI tools for professional purposes.
These Insights promote a second option for those willing to reflect on and steer the development, adoption and effective 
use of GenAI tools for educational purposes, in a curious, critical, responsible and disciplined manner. It not only 
assumes that GenAI tools will remain part of our societies, so that engaging with GenAI and exploring their constructive 
educational use (in balance with many other non‑AI‑related educational activities) will contribute to students’ preparation 
for life, including the labour market. It also recognises that despite the associated risks, if managed carefully and 
responsibly, GenAI tools provide many opportunities that students and teachers can leverage, especially if knowledge 
on the pedagogical use of general‑purpose and educational tools is developed.
Seizing the opportunities of GenAI for education is a shared responsibility among all education stakeholders, from 
parents and families to teachers and students themselves. While the next section presents general guidance to seize 
GenAI opportunities in education, Table 14.2 highlights key pointers for all stakeholders.

Guidance to seize GenAI Opportunities
This section proposed elaborated guidance to support education stakeholders to use GenAI as a tool requiring human 
agency and serving human development. Rather than being driven by technical possibilities, novelty or economic 
opportunities, GenAI tools ought to be developed, used and assessed in education as a means to an educational 
end: serving pedagogical purposes, enriching meaningful learning, fostering equal opportunities, promoting the 
development of human knowledge, skills and wellbeing, and cultivating understanding, critical thinking, creativity and 
civic engagement. As discussed below, they are also expected to be privacy‑preserving, transparent, able to explain their 
outputs, and, to the extent possible, working as effectively for all subpopulations of a country. 
The Insights on the effective use of GenAI in education are organised in 5 sections: 
1. 
Human‑centred teaching and learning with GenAI;
2. 
Investment in GenAI‑related educational R&D;
3. 
Enabling policy environment for trustworthy GenAI in education;
4. 
Effective GenAI infrastructure for all;
5. 
Human agency and human in the loop.
1. Human-centred teaching, learning and assessment with GenAI
Learning and teaching primarily aim to develop valued human knowledge and skills such as independent 
thinking and foundational skills across subjects, while fostering well-being and student agency. This may start 
without GenAI, then with educational GenAI, before incorporating general-purpose GenAI. Used selectively and 
purposefully for pedagogical reasons, GenAI can enrich learning and not replace cognitive effort or weaken the 
human relationships at the heart of education.
GenAI tools offer different opportunities to support teachers to prepare their lessons, to adapt and personalise the 
curriculum to their classes, to design assignments and exams, to help them give more elaborate feedback to their 
students or even to support them in marking the work of their students. They can use educational GenAI tools to 
support student practices, to foster collaborative learning in the classroom and integrate their use by students in 
the learning scenarios they design. GenAI tools can also support teachers to undertake administrative tasks, such as 
documenting their teaching, liaising with parents and students, etc. At all levels of education, teachers have already 
embraced GenAI tools for these purposes to some extent. Their use could be a means to save time that hopefully allows 
them to spend more time and effort on higher level aspects of their teaching, such as building personal relations with 
their students, making their assignments or feedback more personalised or elaborate. In some contexts, GenAI could 
be used to support tutors in real‑time, enhancing the quality of feedback of less experienced tutors.
Students can also enhance their acquisition of knowledge and skills using GenAI as a tool. General‑purpose GenAI 
tools, notably LLMs, provide access to mainstream knowledge in a pre‑digested format. Even if the GenAI output can be 
“hallucinated” at times, and thus be inaccurate, students can ask follow‑up questions and make personalised queries. 
Students already use general‑purpose GenAI tools as a search engine replacement and to get some concepts explained 
to them. They can receive feedback on their ideas and successive drafts, brainstorm, get title ideas, get their texts 
copy‑edited, receive stylistic suggestions, get typos in their computer programmes identified, get ideas to solve a maths 
problem, etc. If they have access to an educational GenAI designed to support their learning rather than merely perform 
tasks, they can be scaffolded in their learning, as would be the case with non‑generative educational AI.
Finally, at the system or institutional level, GenAI can be used to develop standardised assessment items to evaluate 
students’ work, to expand automated assessments to oral tasks, to automatically tag open educational resources and 
make them more easily discoverable by teachers and students, or to provide administrative assistance to students and 
teachers.
These possible benefits come with risks though. The most important one has already been mentioned: if students (or 
teachers) get the entirety of their learning (teaching) tasks done by a general‑purpose GenAI tool, they may be able to 
produce the required output but risk not learning anything in the process. Students (or teachers) need to even more 

Insights on the effective use of generative AI in education
Chapter 14
252
OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026          © OECD 2026
actively engage in their learning when they use GenAI tools. For example, as writing is a thinking task leading writers to 
clarify their intentions and organise their thoughts, asking an LLM to write without personal intellectual engagement in 
the process may hamper students’ thinking (in addition to their writing skills). This is what was referred to as skill atrophy 
in the OECD-EI Guidelines: the lack of continuous use of certain skills may lead to their decline and to the (collective) 
inability to perform certain task without AI tools. In the case of student learning, a more immediate risk is that knowledge 
and skills are not acquired. The risk is amplified with general‑purpose generative AI as educational AI and GenAI tools 
are intentionally designed to support specific aspects of learning (and can usually not be used to perform students’ 
assignments).
At what age is it appropriate to use GenAI tools? To do what? And what kind of AI, general‑purpose or educational? 
These are difficult questions to answer, as it really depends on what GenAI tool is concerned and for what purpose. For 
example, many non‑generative educational AI tools such as intelligent tutoring systems are used in elementary school 
for the learning of mathematics and domestic language; those systems, which have been proven to be effective for 
learning, have become “hybrid” and can now utilise educational GenAI interfaces to make the tools more conversational. 
To the extent that they are effective and safe, there is no reason to discourage their use in primary education. However, 
should elementary school pupils be encouraged to do their homework, if any, with a general‑purpose GenAI? Probably 
not. Most developers forbid the use of those tools below 13 in principle, but new models are being released for younger 
children. Is it possible to use general‑purpose GenAI tools pedagogically with younger children? Possibly yes. GenAI will 
be increasingly part of the fabric of the digital content to which younger children are exposed, and having a teacher 
work with children on the AI generation of images to nurture a class discussion can be a sound pedagogical activity for 
example. While there is still little evidence on the inherent age‑appropriateness of general‑purpose tools, for learning 
this may relate to users’ level of proficiency (and desired proficiency) in the tasks performed with GenAI tools as much as 
to their age. Some level of mastery of the tasks delegated to GenAI tools (foundational knowledge and skills) is necessary 
to exercise critical thinking and judgment on the quality of their outputs, a prerequisite to learn something from using 
it. This is true whatever the student’s age.
Another important risk is the weakening of the essential human relation in education. While GenAI (and AI in general) 
present many opportunities for the personalisation of education, if not properly used GenAI could also lead to more 
impersonal education, with an increasing number of tasks automated or delegated to AI chatbots with almost automatic 
human endorsement. Learning is a social activity where students acquire knowledge about a subject but also learn 
about social interactions at school and in society, skills that will be essential for their future working life and that need to 
be mediated by humans (teachers and other adults). Impersonal education can be desirable for learning in some cases 
though, for example when students are anxious to speak a foreign language and prefer to practice with a conversational 
agent. But an education in which both students and teachers outsource their tasks to GenAI tools may become the ruin 
of education, turning an enterprise of human development into a cycle with no human engagement. 
Always keep in mind that successfully performing a task with GenAI may not involve actual learning. 
The use of (general‑purpose) GenAI may enhance performance in a study task without leading to knowledge acquisition. 
Learning requires the active and often social work of students’ mind. Much of the art of curriculum design and pedagogy 
is to create tasks that will elicit student reasoning and give them opportunities to advance it. None of this can happen 
if the student avoids cognitive effort or thinking. For example, translating a text into a foreign language with an LLM is 
unlikely to correlate with improved mastery of the foreign language. This has also been shown with the use of general‑
purpose GenAI as an adaptive learning system in mathematics or for improving one’s written text. What is in principle 
the product of learning (the proficient achievement of a task) may no longer reflect actual learning if GenAI is involved. 
This does not imply that one cannot learn by using general‑purpose GenAI tools, or that educational GenAI tools have 
the same effect, but the use of GenAI tools should be guided by clear pedagogical objectives or educational purposes. 
Jurisdictions may consider informing and sensitising parents and caretakers to this risk of using general‑purpose 
generative AI tools when supporting their children, as well as the students themselves.

© OECD 2026          OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026

© OECD 2026          OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026 
While teaching subject knowledge, teachers should consider emphasising educational tasks designed 
to intentionally develop valued “human skills” such as reasoning, critical thinking, creativity, 
observation, curiosity as well as social and emotional skills. Providing students with opportunities 
for personal expressions and opinions may make learning more engaging and be more difficult to 
meaningfully outsource to a GenAI tool.
Education institutions aim to develop skills that are socially valued for humans, whether these skills become GenAI 
capabilities or not. The OECD has developed “AI capability indicators” designed to assess and compare AI advancements 
against human abilities. They include creativity, critical thinking and metacognition, and show that AI capabilities are 
progressing in these valued human skills. Even if GenAI could outperform humans on these skills, it would not imply that 
humans should stop valuing and developing them. For example, GenAI can be used to support the creative process and 
the acquisition of creative skills. However, its use has also been shown to reduce collective originality, probably because 
GenAI provides its users with similar suggestions in response to similar requests. Nurturing individual creativity with no 
use of GenAI may thus remain socially beneficial.
Similarly, because GenAI can generate incorrect or not locally appropriate answers, it also helps identify different 
perspectives on a subject: teachers may use GenAI outputs to help develop their students’ critical thinking. However, 
students must also develop critical thinking with no GenAI and learn to think like scientists and navigate uncertainty and 
ambiguity, make and test assumptions, and learn to weigh the strength of evidence.
Requesting students to provide personal insights on a subject, to research and work on topics they are personally 
interested in or to try to understand how they and others feel (empathy) can help mitigate the risk of overreliance on 
GenAI tools as well as nurture personal expression, independent thinking, appreciation of learning and of the world, 
and make educational tasks less standardised and more engaging for students.
Acquiring foundational knowledge and skills in key subjects without the use of general-purpose GenAI 
is needed for students to learn to use GenAI appropriately, for performing complex tasks or just to be 
challenged by GenAI for learning. Teachers may consider providing assignments and exams on the 
foundational knowledge and skills in their field in both closed and open books environments, that is, 
with and without access to GenAI tools. 
As experts using general‑purpose GenAI tools know, GenAI outputs vary from excellent to irrelevant – and the reason 
they know is that they are expert. Students are not experts yet, and they should reach a certain level of expertise in what 
they are studying to know when GenAI outputs should be discarded, improved or used. Expertise is correlated with age, 
especially so when students are younger, but proficiency in what one is supposed to learn trumps age when it comes to 
the use of GenAI. In some instances, teachers may ask students to use GenAI as a scaffold to help them with aspects 
of the task they do not master yet and to focus their attention on the acquisition of skills or knowledge that they are 
closer to mastering. Foundational knowledge that must be mastered for a given field should be assessed with no GenAI 
support. For tasks peripheral to the key learning objectives, enhancing one’s performance with a general‑purpose tool 
is fine (given that the main objective is not about learning the related knowledge and skills). Assessment will also have 
to pay more attention to learning processes rather than just student products.
Assessing student knowledge with or without GenAI can be done in a controlled environment, either by having supervised 
paper and pencil exams or by using digital tools that block or document student use of GenAI tools. It is more difficult 
for tasks that are not meant to be supervised. Beyond the design of assignments that cannot easily be performed by 
GenAI, several models are possible, such as oral examination, the request of short videos rather than, say, short essays, 
a focus on conceptual understanding rather than practical performances. Alternatively, non‑supervised assignments 
can also be used to develop students’ skills in creating or engaging with GenAI tools.

OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026          © OECD 2026
Students are encouraged to use GenAI tools with purpose, within learning scenarios intentionally 
designed by teachers to achieve specific learning goals, taking into account students’ level of mastery 
of the studied subject.
It is a new responsibility for teachers to guide students in using GenAI from time to time as part of their studies. They 
should design some learning activities that involve the use of GenAI, whether general‑purpose or educational. The 
younger and less proficient students are, the more appropriate educational GenAI tools are. When using general‑purpose 
GenAI tools, teachers should design tasks that require cognitive effort and work despite their use. Teachers should also 
support students on how to use these tools: they may request intermediate outputs, prompts, or have access to learning 
analytics documenting the student use of GenAI.
A productive collaboration with GenAI tools can take different forms. It could be about receiving feedback on one’s work, 
but also about evaluating GenAI tools’ outputs in a mindful and critical way. While education systems value students’ 
ability to answer questions and provide solutions, they may now emphasise more students’ ability to ask good questions 
and elicit good answers, by refining their questioning, identifying incorrect or misleading information, knowledge gaps 
or missing perspectives in answers, so as to get balanced and satisfactory answers from GenAI tools (and also humans). 
They may also put more emphasis on the metacognitive skills they are developing.
While the appropriate use of GenAI tools may support the learning of academic knowledge and skills in any subject, 
students also need to develop a certain level of literacy in GenAI itself as part of their digital literacy. The EC‑OECD 
AI literacy framework describes AI literacy as four competences: engaging, creating, managing and shaping AI. This 
literacy includes engagement with a variety of GenAI tools, including for non‑academic purposes, but also encompasses 
understanding the basics of how GenAI works. 
Preparing students to use GenAI does of course not imply that they should use GenAI all the time. As for any other tool 
for learning, teachers should provide students with a variety of learning activities, experiences and scenarios, including 
some with no use of GenAI tools (or technology), and ensure diversity and balance in learning activities. This is essential 
for student wellbeing and engagement.
When using GenAI to develop lesson plans, learning activities, quizzes, exercises, assignments, or 
exams, teachers must continue to exercise their professional judgment and remain responsible for the 
quality and appropriateness of the taught and assessed content.
Like their students, teachers should exercise their evaluative judgment and critical thinking on what GenAI tools produce 
and ensure the produced contents are appropriate for their students in their given context. These time‑saving tools 
are useful to provide teaching ideas, to contextualise courses or personalise them to specific classes, but they may also 
include inaccurate knowledge, misunderstandings of the specific learning contexts, etc. For example, while teachers 
should mobilise their knowledge of how students have and have not been progressing in the classroom to decide which 
topics need revisiting as a priority and which do not, they could use a GenAI tool to generate warm‑up activities bringing 
these topics together. Ideally, if available, teachers should use educational GenAI tools that are aligned with their course 
contents and curriculum rather than general‑purpose GenAI tools.
To maintain a strong human relation in education, teachers are to mostly assess their students 
themselves (without GenAI). When using GenAI tools to help them, exercising their professional 
judgment to evaluate, modify or endorse the AI-generated suggestion is key, not the least to the 
authenticity of the educational relationship.
Providing feedback and assessing the quality of student work is time‑consuming. However, assessment is not an 
administrative task but an essential part of teaching and learning. While technological support can help, especially 
when teaching many students, teachers’ ability to provide personal feedback and motivate their students is bound to 
their personal knowledge of students’ work, their strengths and weaknesses, and a good understanding of their classes. 
GenAI tools open new perspectives for student work assessment. For example, they ease the assessment of assignments 
and exams with rubrics that include multiple explicit assessment dimensions and proficiency descriptions. They also 
allow for the generation of more detailed feedback, which is sometimes found more useful than human feedback (at 
least when the recipient does not know the source). While teachers can take advantage of those new possibilities, 
4

and occasionally automate assessment tasks or subtasks, they should continue to regularly and primarily assess their 
student work themselves and always check and take responsibility for any mark that could have a stake for students’ 
future. The design of GenAI assessment tools could for example ensure that feedback or marks are actively validated 
and thus facilitate teacher agency. GenAI can also be used by students to receive immediate feedback on their work 
when instructors are unavailable, but this cannot replace the professional human feedback of teachers. The social 
dimension of feedback, that is, the knowledge that another person is engaging with the student work, may change the 
way students react, feel, and behave when they produce it. The authenticity of feedback is not only important from the 
student perspective, it is also a professional and moral imperative for teachers.
2. Investment in GenAI-related educational R&D
As general-purpose GenAI tools are not designed specifically for learning, education systems may consider 
supporting the development of tools that aim to enhance teaching and learning. Investing in educational GenAI 
grounded in educational research, co-created with teachers and students, and supported by rigorous research 
on their effectiveness can open new possibilities for educational improvement.
In line with the OECD AI Principles, the OECD‑EI Guidelines emphasised the importance of investing in AI research and 
development. To make AI useful to education, they also called for the involvement of end users at the very beginning of 
the development process. Teachers and students are typically involved at the piloting/testing stage of the development 
process, but rarely at the design stage, when the purpose and functionalities of the AI tools are still to be defined. This 
is the same for GenAI. End users bring practical knowledge and needs that are not necessarily visible to developers or 
academics, hence the value of true “co‑creation”. This section expands the previous guidelines by also highlighting the 
responsibility of EdTech companies when developing tools and highlights current gaps in educational research about 
GenAI for which international co‑operation would be beneficial.
Technology companies and developers are encouraged to develop specialised educational GenAI 
tools based on educational research and pedagogical knowledge. Governments can support them by 
defining clear standards and providing resources and data for the training, configuring or finetuning of 
their educational GenAI systems.
General‑purpose GenAI tools are primarily performance‑ rather than learning‑enhancers. As performance in the 
education sector is mainly about student learning, GenAI developers and technology companies should develop 
GenAI tools meant to support it. Those tools can be designed to be used by students, by teachers, or other education 
stakeholders. Student‑facing learning tools should start from and incorporate insights from educational research and 
pedagogical knowledge while those for teachers should allow them to adjust them based on their pedagogical choices, 
either before or during teaching. For example, teachers may be interested in tools allowing them to easily increase 
the level of hallucinations of a GenAI system used by their students to support their critical thinking. The educational 
orientation of GenAI should undergo impact (or other) evaluations demonstrating their educational value. International 
co‑operation on educational efficacy studies of GenAI use would help advance this agenda. Governments can support 
companies by making some datasets based on their curriculum and education research available, as is the case in 
England (United Kingdom) with the development of a “content store” allowing companies to finetune their GenAI models. 
Developers and companies are expected to test their GenAI tools used in education and ensure they 
are effective, safe for children and students, free of algorithmic bias and respectful of privacy and 
intellectual property. Technology companies and governments could consider working together to 
develop more comprehensive datasets reflecting different historical, cultural or linguistic perspectives.
Because of their generative nature, GenAI tools bring more safety risks when it comes to age‑inappropriate content, 
content not aligned with the curriculum, with educational research or pedagogical knowledge, etc. As key actors in 
the advancement of trustworthy GenAI, developers, and EdTech companies are responsible for the quality, safety, 
and law‑enforcement of their tools. While existing datasets reflect past and current societal perspectives, technology 
companies and governments could collaborate to remedy to the extent possible this technical limitation. They could 
8
7

OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026          © OECD 2026
curate AI training datasets that include a greater variety of perspectives and cultures that are appropriate in students’ 
and teachers’ local context. This was, for example, the ambition of Apertus, an open‑source language model developed 
in Switzerland. Relevant communities should be involved as appropriate in how their languages and cultures are 
represented in these new datasets. As some forms of algorithmic bias are impossible to remove, a regular audit and 
benchmark of educational LLMs could help identify and mitigate them.
The design and development of GenAI tools for educational use should involve teachers as well as 
other stakeholders such as students or parents or teacher unions, as appropriate.
A few countries have launched new initiatives to get end users involved before the late stages of the AI tool development 
process. The objective is to ensure the utility of these tools for education and their subsequent adoption. Governments 
may encourage partnerships between companies, academia and practitioners. In the Netherlands, the government‑
funded National Laboratory on AI (NOLAI) brings together teachers and school representatives with academics, EdTech 
companies and policy makers to design AI tools in a co‑creation process. The French ministry of education also made 
it a requirement of its multi‑step public procurement process of AI tools that companies co‑create their products with 
teachers and students through its AI Innovation partnership (P2IA).
Governments are encouraged to develop internationally comparable metrics and collect data to 
measure AI and GenAI tools usage at all levels of education. Encouraging and funding rigorous 
scientific research with longitudinal or long-intervention designs to assess the impacts of well-defined 
pedagogical uses of GenAI tools on students’ and teachers’ learning and well-being is key, as well 
as continuing funding qualitative and basic research on computer-assisted teaching and learning. 
Working together internationally to research the sound pedagogical and educational uses of GenAI, 
within the OECD and other international fora, involving all stakeholders, will speed up the learning 
process. Finally, jurisdictions and private companies that operate in the public (and government-
dependent) education sector are encouraged to make anonymous, privacy-preserving synthetic 
databases available for research and facilitate their use.
On the research side, there is still a dearth of information about what students and teachers do with GenAI tools for 
educational purposes, what types of tools they use and with what level of satisfaction, how they feel when using them, as 
well as what jurisdictions and schools make available to them. Governments could co‑operate to develop international 
metrics of availability and use of these tools. Research on the effectiveness of GenAI for learning and for productivity 
gain is emerging, but most available experimental research currently lacks statistical power and is focused on short 
interventions that are hardly generalisable to a repeated use of GenAI. Moreover, many research studies on GenAI tools 
do not provide enough specificity about the pedagogical purpose and context of their use, making it difficult to replicate 
or scale them when showing promising effects. While educational GenAI tools are being developed, robust research on 
their effectiveness is needed. All these efforts would contribute to the international knowledge base if providing enough 
information about context. Internationally coordinated educational research studies may also ease the adaption of the 
use of GenAI to educational contexts.
Emerging research on the use of (mainly general‑purpose) GenAI tools points to the need to change learning and 
assessment tasks so they are adapted to the availability of these tools. Educational GenAI tools may mitigate those 
risks and enhance learning, but still need to be meaningfully integrated in teachers’ pedagogical practices. Teachers 
should be encouraged and given the possibility to initiate or participate in research projects about the educational use 
of GenAI tools. This does not imply that all research projects have to be practice‑engaged though. International sharing 
of educational practices and evidence on how to adapt educational tasks and pedagogies so that their use enhances 
(or at least does not hamper) learning will help to more quickly understand and adjust to the digital transformation and 
seize the opportunities brought by GenAI in education.
While research access to educational administrative datasets is possible, it entails privacy risks. The creation of privacy‑
preserving synthetic datasets keeping the characteristics of the real datasets without retaining any personal information 
has now become possible, largely thanks to GenAI. This possibility should be more systematically exploited by 
educational jurisdictions to broaden datasets for education research. Initiatives from other sectors could be examined 
for inspiration. The creation of these privacy‑preserving synthetic datasets should not be limited to administrative 
data but also encompass learning data that are typically collected by private companies, at least partly through public 
contracts.

Higher education institutions are to prepare future scientists and researchers, including education 
researchers, to use and develop specialised scientific GenAI tools.
GenAI is also transforming scientific research: specialised GenAI tools are increasingly available and used to support 
almost all the stages of research, from literature reviews to experimentation through hypothesis generation. Higher 
education institutions should prepare future researchers to use these specialised scientific GenAI tools. Governments 
are advised to also encourage the development of GenAI tools that support educational research specifically and explore 
new avenues they may open for education research.
3. Enabling policy environment for trustworthy GenAI in education
Policy and regulatory frameworks are designed to protect students and support learning while enabling 
innovation. Combined with ongoing stakeholder dialogue, clear expectations on privacy, safety, bias testing, 
age-appropriateness, transparency and alignment with educational objectives can create an enabling 
environment for the trustworthy and meaningful use of GenAI in education.
The challenges and principles for governing GenAI are largely similar to those for non‑generative AI tools. They follow 
the OECD AI Principles: transparency and explainability, robustness, security and safety, and accountability. Other OECD 
standards on privacy and data protection and digital security risk management also apply. The OECD AI Principles 
recommend that governments “shape an enabling policy environment for AI” and that they “review and adapt, as 
appropriate, their policy and regulatory frameworks and assessment mechanisms as they apply to AI systems to 
encourage innovation and competition for trustworthy AI”.
All guidelines from the previous OECD-EI Guidelines remain relevant for GenAI: ethics, safety, privacy and data 
protection, transparency, explainability and negotiation. The ways to enforce these guidelines differ across countries 
and jurisdictions, and can for example be embedded in public procurement practices, the publication of guidance or 
standard expectations.
As part of their digital education governance, most OECD countries have put in place a strong data protection and privacy 
regulation, which is enhanced for minors, with possible different age thresholds for different types of data. Countries in 
the European Union have adopted legislation about the marketability and use of AI, giving education developers some 
obligations before deploying educational GenAI tools. In the case of education, while education objectives and learning 
must prevail, regulatory frameworks have to factor in incentives for EdTech companies to develop affordable, effective 
and equal opportunity digital tools and resources for the education sector. International co‑operation may help make 
the education market less fragmented and more harmonised.
This section casts light on some specific issues associated with GenAI such as safety or lack of comprehensiveness of 
technical algorithmic precision for different contexts (mainly known as “algorithmic bias”).
Jurisdictions and education institutions are expected to transparently inform users about how the 
GenAI tools they use or provide protect users’ data, discussion threads and submitted content. If GenAI 
tools support educational decisions that are high stakes for students (or teachers), the latter should be 
informed about this use in an easy-to-understand way, including the criteria on which the decisions are 
made. Jurisdictions and institutions using such tools may continuously monitor the effectiveness of the 
GenAI tools compared to human decisions and non-generative AI tools.
The first, basic level of transparency is for end users to know that they interact with a GenAI tool rather than with 
a human, unless it is self‑evident. A second aspect lies in how those tools protect the privacy, data and intellectual 
property of their users. While GenAI tools do usually protect the privacy of the data provided by users in their queries 
when used for a fee, this is often not the case for their free versions which may typically be used by students, teachers, 
and education staff (unless GenAI tools are provided by their educational institution). GenAI providers should ensure 
transparent information on whether the user data and queries are collected or used to further train their models. They 
should also aim to be as transparent as possible about how the tools operate, the criteria they use to generate their 
content as well as the datasets on which they were trained.

11

Jurisdictions and educational institutions that provide GenAI tools to education stakeholders should also have the same 
level of transparency with end users and be transparent about their own uses. To the extent possible, if they use AI to 
make or inform decisions, they should explain how the tools are used, and also the methods and criteria used to inform 
their decision. Transparency may also require social dialogue and negotiation of those criteria with teachers and their 
representative organisations, students (and their representative organisations when they exist), parents and families, 
and all other stakeholders. Transparency alone does indeed not guarantee social acceptance of the social tools.
Explainability is difficult to fully achieve with GenAI, even more so than with non‑generative AI. Most GenAI systems 
are proprietary and trained on datasets that are not disclosed, making it challenging to understand the factors that 
shape their outputs. Educational GenAI tools are built on these underlying models and therefore inherit this opacity. 
Nevertheless, explainability remains possible at certain levels: some educational GenAI tools are designed to provide 
information about why and how specific content was generated, including the features considered or the steps taken. 
Such approaches can help strengthen trust and support responsible use, even if they only offer partial explainability.
Governments, together with EdTech companies and other education stakeholders, could work 
internationally to foster the sharing of GenAI practices and policies in education, and encourage 
international, cross-sectoral and open multi-stakeholder initiatives to develop expertise on GenAI. 
This could involve regular convenings, the development of technical standards for interoperable 
and trustworthy GenAI, the development of shared standards or expectations about safe, age-
appropriate tools, joint efforts to reduce algorithmic bias, and common standards for tools aligned with 
pedagogical and educational knowledge. 
Governments share a series of common challenges to ensure the quality, safety and education quality of GenAI tools: 
safety, data protection, alignment with pedagogy, algorithmic bias, etc. They could work internationally, in collaboration 
with GenAI companies, to develop international safety expectations for GenAI tools used in education, as is for example 
the case in England, partially in EU countries through the AI act, or in other countries through their procurement 
processes. They may work with GenAI companies about their transparency in complying with those expectations.
Used for educational purposes by education institutions, GenAI tools should generate safe and age‑appropriate content. 
This risk is usually much lower with non‑generative AI. Beyond GenAI tools used in or for education, non‑educational 
GenAI tools can pose safety risks for students and other stakeholders, for example through new forms of cyber‑bullying 
using their generative affordances in offensive ways. Jurisdictions and education institutions should monitor those risks 
and adapt education systems’ and institutions’ regulations and codes of ethics accordingly. 
GenAI tools also pose greater risks of algorithmic bias. For non‑generative AI, the risks often materialise as AI tools not 
performing equally well for different subpopulations rather than levelling the playing field for all. GenAI tools amplify 
the risks of presentational bias: images, texts or other content that reproduce views considered as inaccurate or 
inappropriate (or locally considered as such). Governments and companies may work together to identify different layers 
of agreement on these so that educational GenAI is aligned with their curriculum and what they consider acceptable 
views within the education sphere. Higher education institutions may fine‑tune GenAI systems so they align with the 
course content and knowledge base suggested by their academic staff.
Similarly, while all countries may not agree on what “good pedagogy” is, given the variety of contexts, they may still 
agree on some basics anchored in educational research, including learning science and all its other sub‑disciplines, 
and develop and share expectations for GenAI tools. This may lead to a multi‑layered set of expectations that different 
countries and jurisdictions could choose from.
Jurisdictions and educational institutions are to continuously update their guidance about the 
responsible uses of GenAI tools by students, teachers, and education staff as well as other stakeholders 
such as parents and caregivers.
Students and families as well as teachers need to receive clear guidance about how GenAI tools can and should be 
used in the learning process. Jurisdictions and educational institutions should consider having a public position about 
the appropriate and inappropriate uses of GenAI, following a dialogue with their students, teachers, staff and their 
representative organisations. Education technology is a socio‑technical system, and a public position based on social 
dialogue will also facilitate further agreement on the responsible uses of GenAI by students as well as teachers. This 
echoes the OECD AI Principles recommendation to “work closely with stakeholders to promote the responsible use of 
AI”. These public positions should be updated regularly given the evolution of those technologies.

This includes providing clear and plain‑language information and supports to parents and caregivers, recognising their 
crucial role in guiding children’s use of GenAI outside of school. Those supports may include glossaries, guidance 
documents, and practical examples to help families understand the possibilities and limitations of GenAI tools, the 
associated risks of overreliance, hallucinations or biased outputs, and the importance of balancing independent learning 
with (hopefully teacher‑guided) GenAI‑assisted tasks. Engaging parents in this dialogue can contribute to more coherent 
expectations across school and home environments, and support more equitable and responsible use of GenAI among 
students. Some countries such as India also provided parents with GenAI applications that support them in inventing 
new stories and reading to their children, which is typically associated with stronger learning outcomes.
Many countries provide such guidance, which should be regularly updated based on emerging evidence on the actual 
use of and research on GenAI in education.
Jurisdictions and educational institutions should provide human alternatives to GenAI, as appropriate, 
and allow those adversely affected by the use of GenAI tools to challenge its outcomes.
The principle of having a human alternative or final resort is as important for GenAI as for non‑generative AI. GenAI 
tools should play a limited and clearly defined role in decision‑making, especially in situations where their use may affect 
individual’s rights (for example, assessment, certification, admissions, disciplinary matters, or comparable tasks). While 
GenAI tools could be the first source of information for some questions or problems, providing the convenience of 
being available at any time of the day while humans may not be, users should be able to ask humans to provide those 
answers when they feel GenAI’s are unsatisfactory. In the (rare) event that GenAI tools are used to make decisions, those 
affected by those decisions or recommendations have to be able to challenge them and get humans back in the loop, 
as noted by the OECD AI Principles.
4. Effective GenAI infrastructure for all
Jurisdictions typically ensure that all students and teachers can benefit from GenAI thanks to digital 
infrastructure and support accessible to all (devices, connectivity, digital resources and professional learning 
opportunities). Providing curriculum-aligned GenAI resources, alternative solutions where divides persist, and 
sustained professional learning enables effective and meaningful uses of GenAI in education.
The opportunities of GenAI for education and learning rely on access to an adequate and affordable digital infrastructure, 
including digital devices, high‑quality connectivity services and infrastructures, educational GenAI tools and other digital 
resources as well as qualified teachers who know how to use them appropriately for teaching and student learning. 
Ensuring a level playing field ensures that talented students are not held back by lack of basic infrastructure.
High‑quality connectivity is usually a necessary prerequisite to support the high throughput (download and upload 
speeds) and low latency (i.e.  minimal delays in the round‑trip time for a response) required for GenAI to deliver 
responses in real‑time. However, ensuring that all in society have access to high‑quality and affordable communication 
services everywhere is still aspirational in many cases. Eliminating broadband connectivity divides and ensuring high‑
quality digital infrastructure at affordable prices for everyone, in all locations, is a first step to providing equality of 
opportunities to students from all socio‑economic backgrounds and geographical origins. The OECD Recommendation 
on Broadband Connectivity underlines the importance of eliminating divides in access to high‑quality and affordable 
broadband services as well as in the digital skills needed to make effective use of applications that leverage them, such 
as GenAI tools.
The advice in this section adapts the previous OECD‑EI Guidelines to the case of GenAI, and also includes suggested 
actions on teacher professional learning. Non‑generative educational AI tools such as intelligent tutoring systems were 
largely not available for free to students and teachers, and therefore usually not accessible unless provided through 
their educational institution. This is not the case for general‑purpose GenAI tools, which are available for free regardless 
of institutional provision, and whose most powerful versions are available for a fee to the students and teachers who 
can afford them.
As mentioned throughout this document, education policy makers and other stakeholders should consider two main use 
cases for GenAI tools: a supervised and controlled use in and for the classroom as part of a teacher‑designed learning 
activity, and educational uses by students and teachers that are unplanned by education institutions and stakeholders.
15

Insights on the effective use of generative AI in education

260
OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026          © OECD 2026
In addition to access to adequate devices and connectivity services and infrastructures and GenAI resources, students 
and teachers need the relevant skills to use GenAI tools for learning. This can be facilitated by access to skilled teachers, 
administrators and peers that have a high level of proficiency to use such tools in their educational practices. This 
involves the provision of learning opportunities to all stakeholders but also the investment in support staff that can 
provide coaching and mentoring about the pedagogical and administrative uses of GenAI tools. Those opportunities 
can take different forms, from teacher education to formal professional learning activities through to the building of 
teacher professional learning communities around the use of GenAI tools. 
Jurisdictions are encouraged to ensure that all students and teachers have access to quality devices 
and connectivity for educational purposes, within and outside of educational institutions, a prerequisite 
for them to experience, learn about and benefit from GenAI tools.
Closing broadband connectivity divides, as well as broader digital divides is a challenge that goes beyond education, but 
remains an important priority to ensure the adoption and effective use of GenAI in education. This is a pre‑condition for 
any use of AI for educational purposes. The OECD Recommendation on Broadband Connectivity provides recommendations 
to help bridge these digital divides, promote widespread broadband deployment and foster competition and investment 
in broadband development. The quality and reliability of connectivity is a key element of access. In education, quality 
devices need to be adequate for learning applications and have sufficient performance, including long enough battery 
life, be long lasting and abide by sustainability standards. This does not imply that public authorities have to pay for 
devices and connectivity for all students. Leases, loans, zero‑rating of specific sites and other solutions have been 
successfully experienced in the past years in different countries and jurisdictions. If publicly provided, devices should be 
affordable, measured by the total cost of ownership. Among many possible models, Ceibal in Uruguay has developed a 
long experience in the provision and support of educational devices for all their public‑school students.
Digital learning resources and tools made available to students, teachers and other education 
stakeholders are expected to include educational LLMs and other generative AI tools. Educational 
GenAI tools specifically developed for education may be privileged, even though older students also 
have to engage with general-purpose GenAI tools. Where it is challenging to quickly address disparities 
in equipment and connectivity, jurisdictions may consider “AI Unplugged” models and provide (or 
publicise existing) Small Language Models (SLMs) and other smaller versions of GenAI models.
General‑purpose LLMs and other tools are usually not educational in purpose. Jurisdictions and institutions may consider 
providing access to GenAI tools that are aligned with their curriculum, courses, pedagogical preferences and other 
educational objectives. This provision is also a way to provide tools that respect privacy and data protection. Typically, 
a mix of general‑purpose and educational GenAI tools will be most helpful. Depending on the task, they may consider 
whether non‑generative educational AI tools would not be more effective or appropriate. One challenge for education 
lies in the cost of licensing privacy‑preserving GenAI tools for students and teachers, but many countries, jurisdictions 
or education institutions already do so.
Some countries, jurisdictions and higher education institutions have adopted different approaches. England has 
developed a content store providing EdTech developers resources to finetune their educational GenAI models so they 
align with the English curriculum and research evidence about teaching. France is developing a “sovereign AI” for 
teachers and students that aligns with its values and curriculum and respects privacy. Korea has introduced AI‑powered 
digital teaching and learning materials that blend traditional resources with pedagogically validated AI digital tools. 
These materials are designed for targeted use by students and teachers across specific school levels and subject areas. 
As part of its AI Leap programme, Estonia is working with GenAI companies and licensed general‑purpose GenAI tools 
for teachers and an educational version for their high school students. Some higher education institutions across the 
world have also either developed their own GenAI tools to support their students and teachers or provided access to 
commercial models while ensuring their privacy, intellectual property and data protection. 
Given the current reality of persistent connectivity and digital divides, jurisdictions and educational institutions can 
also consider the “AI unplugged” model. This approach consists of using AI tools and resources that work with existing 
digital connectivity infrastructure (usually mobile phone or smartphones) and level of digital skills. Brazil has for example 
successfully used it in some areas of the country where devices and connectivity are scarcely available. In the case of 
GenAI, Small Language Models run on mobile phones offline and can provide students and teachers with a first access 
to AI language models, although with limited capabilities compared to the large ones. It would be welcome that GenAI 
companies develop small GenAI models for educational purposes, and that jurisdictions make education stakeholders 
aware of them where appropriate.

Jurisdictions and education institutions are to provide teachers with continuous professional learning 
opportunities about the use of GenAI in education, mostly the pedagogical use of GenAI, but also the 
basics of how the technology works, its possibilities and limitations, and its societal and environmental 
impacts. Knowledge about the pedagogical use of GenAI tools can be acquired in pre-service teacher 
education and regularly updated through continuous professional learning opportunities. Jurisdictions 
are also encouraged to support education institutions and teachers in the selection and use of GenAI 
tools for education.
Teachers’ GenAI pedagogical literacy can come from a variety of professional learning opportunities, in pre‑service 
teacher education as well as during in‑service learning opportunities. As for any other professional knowledge, it comes 
from learning by doing and thus from the access and use of GenAI tools for some professional purposes as well as from 
different types of real‑time human support, which may range from “digital” or “AI” champions and professional learning 
communities through to innovation projects focused on the use of GenAI for teaching and student learning. Teachers 
should acquire enough professional knowledge to make informed decisions as to when GenAI tools should and should 
not be used, and how they can best support student learning.
For teachers, GenAI literacy also encompasses the ability to use GenAI tools in their teaching to support their students’ 
learning. They should gain a basic understanding of GenAI as a technology, including its strengths and limitations, and 
learn how to effectively and ethically use it. The AI literacy framework published by the European Commission and the 
OECD could support this effort.
Jurisdictions are well placed to support teachers and administrators to keep abreast of new developments in the 
landscape of educational GenAI tools and inform and curate them so they can more easily select and appropriately use 
them. This curation should consider non‑generative educational AI tools that may be more effective or appropriate than 
GenAI tools for similar use cases. Teachers also need support to navigate the ethical, legal and pedagogical issues that 
arise when students and families use generative AI beyond the classroom.
Jurisdictions may consider the ethical provision and use of trustworthy educational GenAI tools by 
teachers for their professional development.
AI tools such as classroom analytics provide teachers with feedback about some aspects of their teaching, with no 
intrusion of a human observer, but also with significant risks of unethical use by their employers. For example, these 
tools can record how much time teachers have spoken during class, what mix of pedagogical activities or learning 
strategies they have used, etc. GenAI tools can help turn the analysis of these classroom observations into suggestions 
and recommendations, sometimes in real‑time, but most often after class. This feedback would allow teachers to reflect 
on and improve their practice. While research is still underway, this GenAI feedback may be more impactful when it 
is discussed with a coach or mentor who has not observed the class (nor made the initial suggestions). Jurisdictions 
and developers are expected to ensure these tools do serve professional learning and not surveillance, for example by 
limiting access to the collected information to the interested teachers only.
5. Human agency and human in the loop
Human judgment, relationships and responsibility should not be inadvertently replaced by GenAI, even though 
some educational tasks can be purposefully automated. Designing educational GenAI tools and practices that 
preserve human oversight, and fostering dialogue on what may and may not be automated, can support more 
trustworthy, equitable and educationally meaningful uses of GenAI.
Both non‑generative AI and GenAI can be used to automate some educational tasks performed by teachers, students, 
administrators or other stakeholders – even though it cannot lead to an automation of educational occupationq as a 
whole in the foreseeable future. Human judgment, relationships or responsibility should not be inadvertently delegated to 
GenAI tools, even though some educational tasks could purposefully be automated. The OECD-EI Guidelines highlighted 
the importance of keeping a “human in the loop” and, when possible, a human alternative to digital tools or processes. 
This is key to implementing the human‑centred values of the OECD AI Principles. The above insights already include this 
focus on human agency. This section concludes the document by emphasising this key dimension.
As mentioned above, GenAI has the potential to automate some time‑consuming teaching, learning, assessment and 
administrative tasks and, in principle, allow teachers and education staff to redirect their efforts to more important 
18
19

Insights on the effective use of generative AI in education
Chapter 14
262
OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026          © OECD 2026
learning, teaching or administrative tasks, including relational ones. Still, in most cases, the human agency and oversight 
of students, teachers and administrators when using GenAI is essential. Students need to be agents of their learning 
for actual learning to happen. Teachers also need to be agents of their teaching to continue to learn professionally 
and engage students in learning – and avoid skill atrophy as a result of uncritically implementing content generated by 
GenAI tools. Institutions might consider annual “automation and agency” audits that would lead actors to reflect on what 
tasks or subtasks they have automated and how they exercise their agency. Developers should ensure that teachers 
remain active by designing GenAI tools in ways that maintain this agency when necessary, for example by making them 
co‑design some GenAI tools, allow them to customise the AI tools as they wish, or to validate the outputs generated by 
the AI tools. While human agency can imply to revise or discard GenAI outputs, it also has to be supported by specific 
design features of GenAI tools. Education researchers should also use GenAI with judgment, imagination and critical 
thinking, as is the case for all scientists.
The importance of human agency increases when stakes get higher for those affected by the actions or decisions of the 
GenAI tools. The versatility of GenAI tools may lead humans to become over‑confident in GenAI accuracy and overreliant 
on it. Even when they perform extremely well most of the time, GenAI tools may have some level of hallucinations, make 
mistakes, lack consistency over time – or just not have the expected effects as human actions because of the relational 
dimension of education. As a result, humans must exercise their agency, double check and critically evaluate their 
outputs, especially if social stakes are attached to them. 
A dialogue on what should and should not be automated is therefore needed. While human agency is key, its 
implementation is a distributed responsibility across all AI actors and stakeholders of the education eco‑system: 
governments and jurisdictions, education institutions, students and teachers, as well as companies developing GenAI 
tools. Keeping human agency at the centre of GenAI use, together with thoughtful decisions about the appropriate 
degree of automation, can support more educationally meaningful, effective, equitable and trustworthy uses of GenAI 
in education.

For further reading
The Insights on the effective use of generative AI in Education mainly build on existing research evidence as well as new 
ongoing development projects of educational GenAI tools. They also build on the expertise of academics, country officials, 
the OECD Secretariat and education stakeholders. Most of the underlying research and evidence in the document will be 
found in the following publication:
OECD (2026), OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026: Exploring Effective Uses of Generative AI in Education, OECD Publishing, 
Paris, https://doi.org/10.1787/062a7394‑en.
Some aspects were also derived from previous OECD work on education or on other sectors than education. The Insights 
supplement the Opportunities, guidelines and guardrails for effective and equitable use of AI in education (OECD-EI Guidelines), 
co‑published by the OECD and Education International (2023). They also supplement the AI literacy framework for primary and 
secondary education co‑published by the European Commission and the OECD (2025). The document also builds on a review 
of member country guidelines and frameworks as well as international guidelines, such as those published by the European 
Commission, UNESCO or UNICEF. Guidelines developed by higher education institutions in countries were also analysed. Last 
but not least, the Insights build on the updated OECD Council Recommendations on Broadband Connectivity (2021) and on 
Artificial Intelligence (2024) (OECD AI Principles). The following references are meant for readers who want to deepen their 
knowledge about OECD work on AI and the digital transformation.

OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026
Exploring Effective Uses of Generative AI in Education
The OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026 explores emerging research on the use of generative AI in education 
and presents innovative tools and applications that show promise. The report examines the use of generative AI 
in different teaching and learning scenarios: by students to learn subject knowledge, by students and teachers together 
as part of instruction, and by teachers alone to support their work in the classroom. The Outlook also showcases how 
generative AI can enhance the efficiency of education institutions and systems, such as research, analysis of learning 
pathways and support for study advisors. While highlighting the opportunities and benefits of generative AI, the report 
also notes key challenges and concerns. It provides a state‑of‑the‑art overview of the impact and possibilities 
of generative AI in education and is an essential resource for education policymakers, institution leaders, researchers, 
as well as other stakeholders.
